title: The Girl Who Saved the Rainbow Floor
markdown:
Not all grand adventures begin with a trumpet fanfare. Some start with a quiet afternoon and a missing splash of colour.

It was after school, the kind of golden afternoon where sunlight streamed through the tall windows of Oakwood Elementary and the polished floors gleamed like a freshly polished apple. June, a girl whose brain buzzed with more inventions than a beehive had bees, walked the main corridor, footsteps echoing. Her pockets jingled with spare cogs and little springs, just in case inspiration struck. June liked to be prepared for a sudden urge to build.

She paused. Her usual bright smile faded a little. The magnificent mosaic floor — blues like a summer sky, greens like a deep forest, fiery reds like a dragon’s breath — looked wrong. Right in the middle, where a proud lion was supposed to roar in a thousand tiny stones, there was grey. Plain, boring grey, a cloudy day with no sunshine. A tremor of concern.

“Oh dear. Ketu?”

A rustle of wind filled the corridor, not gusty, not scary — a playful one that tickled the potted plants. Down from the skylight, soaring on silent shimmering wings, came Ketu. Not just any kite. A dragon of sun-kissed silk, scales that caught the light like tiny jewels, a tail that whipped with gentle grace. He landed beside June, amber eyes blinking slowly.

“What is it, June?” The soft sigh of wind through pines. “You sound troubled.”

“Look. The floor. Pieces are gone. The lion is hurt.”

Ketu lowered his silken head and nudged a small bright blue shard, then a fleck of fiery red, then, by the coat rack, a sliver of forest green.

June felt a flutter, the familiar feeling when things did not quite fit. Gears that had not meshed. Not quite fear. A wobbly uncertainty. She liked things complete, like a perfectly built clock. This was not complete.

Just as they were puzzling, the stern but kindly Headmaster, Mr. Finch, came striding down, sensible shoes clip-clop. His eyebrows shot up as if they were surprised guests. “Good heavens, June. The mosaic. A dreadful state.”

He wrung his hands, dry leaves. “I was just about to tell the caretakers to lay down that old carpet from the storeroom. Repairs won’t be done until next week. The children start back tomorrow morning. A rug will have to do.”

June’s heart sank. A rug over their broken rainbow. She imagined children walking a dull grey carpet, missing all the stories the mosaic told. Mr. Finch muttered, almost to himself, “If only someone could find those missing bits before tomorrow.”

June stood a little taller. Her inventor’s brain, usually busy with automatic toast-buttering machines and self-tying shoelaces, whirred a different plan. “Mr. Finch. Ketu and I will find them. All the missing pieces.”

Mr. Finch blinked. “You, June? Ambitious. Bless your inventive heart. You have a week — no. Before morning assembly tomorrow. The rug is waiting.” A ticking clock, bigger than the one on her workshop desk.

The wobbly uncertainty stayed, but a spark of determination sat beside it. “We’ll do our best, sir.” She met his gaze.

The quest began. June, with Ketu soaring gently overhead to guide her, his shimmering form a beacon in the dim corridors, started searching. They looked in every nook and cranny. They peered under benches where forgotten lunchboxes sometimes hid. They investigated shadowy corners behind forgotten art projects that smelled faintly of glue and paint. Ketu’s hawk-sharp eyes could spot the smallest glimmer. A blue chip by the drinking fountain. A gold fleck in a crack by the gym doors. June’s pockets grew heavier, and still the lion’s middle stayed grey.

“These pieces are so small,” June said, picking a sun-yellow sliver near the lost-and-found. Smooth and cool. “Why make such beautiful art out of so many little bits?”

Ketu, who remembered overheard conversations and dusty library books, said, “Those little bits are called tesserae. I recall an old book about Roman history. The ancient Romans used them for their grand mosaics. Each tiny piece, carefully placed, built a picture. A story. A whole world.”

“Tesserae.” The word felt important on her tongue. Not just a lost tile. A tiny echo of an ancient artist. A whisper from the past.

Their search led to the back of the old storage room, so forgotten even the dust seemed ancient. Behind a stack of wobbly cardboard boxes, a dusty wooden box, hinges stiff. Full of them. Hundreds of tiny colourful tesserae, like fallen jewels, cool surfaces whispering as they shifted, smelling of dust and forgotten time. A faded note in looping elegant handwriting: To the next caretakers of our beautiful floor. These are the tesserae, the heart of our mosaic. Sometimes they wander, but they always find their way home. — A Grateful Student, 1952.

June picked up a deep red tessera, a tiny polished pebble. “We found them. And look. A message.” The wobble vanished, replaced by a warm steady feeling, sunshine after rain. She had promised. She had searched dusty corners. She had spoken up.

With Ketu’s gentle help they worked through the late afternoon, the hallway filled with a quiet sense of purpose. June, pockets now full of tesserae instead of spare parts, carefully placed each tiny piece back into its rightful spot. Blue of the mane. Red of the fierce eyes. Gold of the regal pose. A few would not sit until she turned them the way the old student must have turned them. The lion began to roar again, colours vibrant and strong.

The next morning the children filed in, chatter fading as they walked the main corridor, and they gasped. The grey patch was gone. The mosaic shimmered, a magnificent rainbow under their feet. June stood beside it, pockets empty, heart full.

She told Mr. Finch about Ketu, the tesserae, and the note from 1952. His stern expression softened. “June. You are a true inventor — not just of machines, but of solutions. You saved our rainbow.”

Ketu fluttered his silken wings a little higher. June’s hands, empty of cogs for once, were dusty with old stone and new pride. The lion held. The rug stayed in the storeroom.
